newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-Australian Q2 net foreign debt.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-Australian Q2 net foreign debt.

text.p: Australia's net foreign debt at the end of the June quarter was A$187.804 billion, the Australian Bureau of Statistics said.
Economists had been expecting a figure around A$186 billion, and the June quarter figure was a rise on the revised March quarter figure of A$185.155 billion.
A selection of economists immediate reactions to the data are listed below.
TIM MOLONEY, ECONOMIST, COMMONWEALTH BANK OF AUSTRALIA:

"These statistics are moving in the right direction (for a sovereign credit-ratings upgrade)," he said, adding the result was broadly in line with market expectations. "Looking at net debt as a proportion of GDP, there was a slight improvement in the June quarter. On net debt servicing costs as a proportion of exports, there's a further improvement to 11.3 percent (compared with around 20 percent in the early 1990s)."
STEPHEN KOUKOULAS, SENIOR ECONOMIST, CITIBANK AUSTRALIA:

"It's mildly encouraging to see net debt appearing to be relatively steady as a share of GDP...but it is still high and still leaves us vulnerable to any external shocks given our high level of debt, and it probably reinforces the fiscal strategy of moving to surpluses as quickly as possible."
AKIS HARALABOPOULOS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, GIO AUSTRALIA:

"The market hasn't reacted, I suspect, purely because the ratio of net investment income to exports, which is what it costs Australia to fund that net debt, has fallen once again to 11.3 percent. As far as your big picture long term is concerned we're still susceptible to swings in commodity prices and interest rates - the bigger your debt the more susceptible you are."
DAVID BASSANESE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, BANKERS TRUST:

"June last year 39.9 (percent of GDP), June this year 38.6 so it's sort of consistent with the idea that we're seeing a plateauing in the foreign debt, helped obviously by the strength of the exchange rate this year. The other important point to bring out...is that public debt is only a fraction of this. The bottom line of it all is that as a percent of GDP, net debt has been coming down, helped by the strength of the exchange rate rate, but also we've had an improvement in the current account."
ROB HENDERSON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, DRESDNER AUSTRALIA:

"We are starting to see the benefits of lower interest rates. Public sector net debt dropped 1.3 percent in this quarter ... I think this is a timely reminder of why we are going through all this (fiscal) pain ... I guess the fact that our debt levels as a percentage of GDP has stablisied now, combined with much better prospects of the government's fiscal position -- this only enhances the chances of a credit upgrade down the track."
